item.title: Town in S China's Guangdong turns knitwear industry into global success story
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Town in S China's Guangdong turns knitwear industry into global success story Dalang, a town of less than 100 square kilometers in Dongguan city, south China's Guangdong Province, produces about 900 million sweaters a year, roughly one in every five sweaters made worldwide. The town's complete sweater industrial chain generates annual trade of more than 72 billion yuan ($10.6 billion). At the Dalang Knitwear Trade Center, Zhang Jiankai, head of a supply chain management company, recently used the Dongguan Market Procurement Trade Network Information Platform to ship a batch of women's sweaters to an Australian buyer. Photo shows a factory in Dalang, Dongguan, south China's Guangdong Province. (Photo/China Economic Weekly) Zhang and many other industry veterans who have worked in the town for more than a decade credit Dalang's rise to its complete local supply chain. Raw materials, skilled workers and designers are all within a few kilometers, and the town's export channels reach more than 160 countries and regions. Zhong Jinfa, an official in Dalang, said the town's knitwear industry began in the late 1970s. Over the past 40-plus years, competition has pushed the sector toward digital upgrading, backed by local government subsidies for equipment upgrades and model factories. The town's factories now operate 150,000 flat knitting machines, including more than 10,000 advanced computerized models. At the China Dalang Woolen Knitwear Fair, held from June 24 to 26, an AI-powered design tool drew attention. Trained on a database of more than 2 million knitwear patterns, it lets designers generate multiple design options in one to two minutes by entering keywords, cutting design costs by more than 60 percent. Combined with smart manufacturing, the tool has cut prototyping time from three days to two hours, enabling flexible, made-to-order production in Dongguan and helping innovative designs quickly become bestsellers. Dongguan Tongfa Knitwears Co., Ltd. is betting on quality over volume. "Dalang's knitwear industry is shifting away from labor-intensive, high-volume production. Our company, for example, has focused on the high-end segment, with sales growing 20 to 30 percent a year," said Liu Dianyu, the company's chairman. About 70 percent of its products are exported to Europe and the U.S., with unit factory prices of $25 to $30. "Sweaters today are worn for fashion, not just warmth," said Liu, who has built a design team of more than 100 people, or a third of the company's staff. Research and development accounts for half of total costs, and the company plans to open a design studio in Europe. Innovation is also extending to materials. Firms in Dalang develop nearly 10,000 new yarn products each year. They hold more than 200 yarn-related patents, with fancy-yarn patents accounting for roughly two-thirds of China's total. "Driven by advances in technology, business models and materials, Dalang's knitwear industry is accelerating its move up the value chain," said Ye Jianfen, deputy head of Dalang town. Policy support has helped smaller traders reach global markets. Since 2020, Dalang has piloted a "market procurement trade" model that simplifies customs declarations and exempts small, mixed-category orders from value-added tax invoicing, with a cap of $150,000 per customs declaration, according to Liu Haojiang, head of the Dalang Market Procurement Trade Service Center. "For a small trading company like ours to sell sweaters to 30 or 40 countries, we've relied heavily on a good business environment and thoughtful policy support, especially the simplified export procedures and improved services," Zhang said. The model now covers categories beyond wool products, including footwear, luggage, plastics, toys and hardware. As of July 18, Dalang's market procurement exports this year had reached 13.11 billion yuan, with cumulative exports of 220.06 billion yuan reaching buyers in 225 countries and regions. "We'll continue supporting the healthy growth of new trade models, including market procurement trade," said Liu Rui, a local customs officer, adding that the goal is to help more Chinese-made knitwear reach global markets. item.title: China's robots: Don't just watch, understand the industrial system
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
China's robots: Don't just watch, understand the industrial system Illustration: Chen Xia/GT A Chinese humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds to beat the men's 100m world record of 9.58 seconds set by Usain Bolt. This feat, achieved during the opening ceremony of the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, quickly captured global headlines. The second World Humanoid Robot Games offered a vivid window into the country's fast-moving robotics industry. Images of humanoid machines running, balancing, navigating obstacles and performing coordinated tasks naturally attract attention. Such events reveal something significant: China has become exceptionally capable of translating advances in components, controls, software integration and manufacturing into physical machines that can be built, tested and improved at speed. The value of these competitions lies less in a single headline-grabbing performance than in the industrial system behind it. A humanoid robot on a track is the visible result of motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, structural materials, motion-control systems, embedded software, training data, assembly processes and field maintenance working together. China's advantage increasingly lies in its ability to coordinate the entire supply chain. It has a broad base of electronics and machinery suppliers, strong manufacturing capacity, dense industrial clusters, and a large pool of potential users willing to test robots in factories, warehouses, ports, shops, hospitals and service settings. Competitions can therefore serve as public demonstrations and stress tests for a wider ecosystem. This development has occurred amid expanding US restrictions on China's access to advanced technologies, particularly leading-edge semiconductors, high-performance computing equipment and certain software and manufacturing tools. These measures have had real effects. They raise costs, complicate supply chains and make it harder for Chinese firms to obtain some of the most advanced chips and technical capabilities. Robotics increasingly depends on artificial intelligence, high-performance processors and sophisticated development tools, and US containment policy has challenged China's robotics development. Yet the restrictions have not stopped China's robotics industry from growing. One reason is that industrial competitiveness is not determined by frontier chips alone. In many robotics applications, the decisive challenge is making a system reliable, affordable, maintainable and safe in real operating conditions. China's large and varied domestic market provides companies with unusually frequent opportunities to confront these challenges. A robot deployed in a logistics center, manufacturing workshop or pharmacy generates feedback that can improve design, software, hardware integration and service procedures. This creates a reinforcing cycle: More applications produce more operational data and experience; better products reduce costs and increase confidence; and lower costs support wider deployment. Scale matters as well. China's manufacturing ecosystem enables firms to move from prototype to small-batch production and then to larger-scale delivery relatively quickly. That process can accelerate learning not only for robot makers but also for suppliers of actuators, sensors, machine vision systems, batteries and precision components. The result is not simply a lower-cost version of foreign technology. It is a growing capacity to adapt products to diverse use cases and to iterate rapidly when products encounter real-world constraints. This has implications beyond China. As robots become more available and affordable, they can help manufacturers globally address labor shortages, improve workplace safety and raise productivity in repetitive or hazardous tasks. Chinese firms can contribute equipment, components and competitive pressure that expand the overall market and reduce barriers to adoption. In this sense, China's robotics progress may become part of a broader modernization of global manufacturing rather than a purely national achievement. However, a balanced assessment requires acknowledging the remaining gaps. The US retains major strengths in foundational artificial intelligence research, advanced semiconductors, computing platforms and software ecosystems. Japan and several European countries remain highly competitive in precision components, industrial reliability, specialized automation, safety systems and technical standards. China still faces challenges in certain high-end chips, core software, advanced sensors, precision parts, long-term reliability, and internationally recognized standards and certification. China's recent robotics events deserve attention because they illustrate a broader industrial fact. Despite external technological constraints, China has leveraged its domestic market, supply-chain depth, engineering talent and manufacturing scale to strengthen its position in robotics. Its advantage lies not in claiming technological supremacy in every category, but in its growing ability to turn innovation into deployment. If China can continue to close its remaining gaps while remaining open to global collaboration and standards, its robotics industry could become an important contributor to the next phase of worldwide industrial development. item.title: Protectionism is the last thing European automakers need
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
GT Voice: Protectionism is the last thing European automakers need Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Sebastian Lechner, state chairperson of the Christian Democratic Union in Germany's Lower Saxony, has called for the EU to quickly impose import tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, Reuters reported on Friday. For some time, European media have reported that the European Commission plans to impose countervailing duties on such vehicles, which will amplify concerns over China-EU trade tensions. As the home to Volkswagen's global headquarters, Lower Saxony has been bearing the brunt of industrial restructuring amid the global energy transition. So, the politician's call for imposing tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars is essentially an attempt to curry favor with local manufacturers and local workers in exchange for gaining political support from them. But turning the operational pressure of local carmakers into political demand to erect trade barriers will not solve Germany's industrial problems. On the contrary, protectionism will almost certainly steer German auto sector further down the wrong path. For years, a number of European politicians and industry players have attributed the rapid growth of Chinese new-energy vehicles to the so-called "subsidies," hoping that erecting higher tariffs can shield European carmakers from global competition. Yet, the growing popularity of Chinese hybrid vehicles in the European market stems from nothing but their perfect alignment with the most pressing consumer demands. For starters, it's very expensive for ordinary European consumers to replace vehicles due to the persistently high prices of local cars. The EU has unveiled a plan to drop the ban on new combustion-engine cars from 2035, which would allow continued sales of non-electric vehicles including plug‑in hybrids (PHEVs). Market acceptance of PHEVs is relatively high in Europe. As a matter of fact, Chinese PHEVs have helped fill a critical market gap and provided European consumers with a pragmatic and affordable low-carbon mobility solution. Resorting to protection by imposing higher trade tariffs will deprive European consumers of the right to buy high-quality and cost-effective cars. If anything, the market performance following the EU's imposition of new tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) has already proven that trade protectionism only delivers limited effects in the long run. A report published by The Guardian revealed this month that despite EU tariffs of up to 35.3 percent on the EVs made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10-percent import duty, Chinese EV sales have still risen across Europe to hit a record high. The share of EVs sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2 percent across western European markets - or one in every seven EVs - in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. Following a brief sales drop caused by tariff shocks, Chinese cars have quickly regained growth momentum, as their appeal to European consumers who favor affordable, high‑quality electric mobility has not changed. If the EU extends protectionist measure to Chinese PHEVs, European consumers will bear the full brunt of higher prices. Elevated prices could erase the new energy consumption push in Europe. The European auto market, which has just begun to show signs of recovery, will once again be dragged into a prolonged slump by protectionism. According to China Automotive News, more than 40 percent of the complete vehicles exported from China to the EU market come from joint ventures or wholly foreign‑owned factories in China. That means for every five cars shipped to Europe, roughly two are produced by European or other foreign manufacturers - including BMW and Mercedes‑Benz, all of which rely on China's mature supply chains to build highly competitive models and ship them back to Europe. Imposing punitive duties on these vehicles would raise their costs and disrupt their integrated production strategies. In addition, China's stance on tackling trade issues with the EU has always been clear. In May, a spokesperson from China's Ministry of Commerce said that China will take resolute countermeasures if the EU insists on imposing discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies. Ultimately, the competitiveness of the global auto industry is never decided by tariffs. The race toward electrification and intelligence is one of technological innovation, supply‑chain efficiency, and cost control. Tariff pushes by certain politicians may win favor from local workers, yet they will trap Europe's automotive industry in a vicious cycle of protectionism. In the long run, such short-sighted moves will undermine the long-term vitality and competitiveness of European carmakers. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert Yin Yuzhen is reunited with Ronald Sakolsky at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a visit aimed at renewing a friendship with the Chinese people that first took root more than two decades ago. The 69-year-old will spend part of his stay planting trees alongside his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades. Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification. At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life. The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees. In May this year, Yin took to the internet in search of the American friend who had offered the donation decades ago, and their online reunion, a moment that moved many, soon followed. On May 18, the two finally connected over a video call. Yin, who had been practicing over and over, greeted him in her slightly broken English: "You are brother!" Upon arriving in Beijing, Sakolsky said he was eager to meet Yin in northern China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, reconnect with former colleagues and students, and see the forest with his own eyes. He also received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the desert. Ahead of Sakolsky's arrival in Inner Mongolia on Sunday afternoon, Yin, no less excited, brought with her pepino melons freshly picked from her orchard. "I went to pick some pepino melons for him, so he can taste the fruit from the desert the moment he steps off the plane," she said. "When I tell him I grew these in the desert, he won't believe it." Yin Yuzhen waves to Ronald Sakolsky at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) At the Ordos Ejin Horo Airport in Inner Mongolia, as soon as Yin spotted him coming down the escalator, she rushed to him. Overcome with emotion, the two hugged tightly, weeping with joy after more than two decades apart. "This is a dream come true," said Sakolsky. "She made a promise 27 years ago and she kept her promise. I never thought I would see her again. It is a miracle, but it shows culture and people can still keep promises." Invited by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), his itinerary from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1 will also include China-U.S. teacher exchange events, a visit to Henan to meet with teachers and students at the school where he worked, a visit to the press briefing hall of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and visits to historical and cultural landmarks. The invitation is intended to further promote China-U.S. educational exchanges, convey the Chinese people's deep appreciation of friendship, and inspire more people to carry forward heartwarming stories of goodwill between the two peoples, a CEAIE official said. Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns. Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students. Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu (about 10.13 million hectares) of sandified land between 2021 and 2025. item.title: China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
China's global initiatives offer new opportunities for cooperation, says Italian business leader Guests attend the 4th China-Italy Friendship Cities Cooperation Dialogue in Rome, Italy, April 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Jing) ROME, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The China-proposed four global initiatives offer a new perspective on international governance and new opportunities for international cooperation amid geopolitical fragmentation and global instability, said an Italian business leader. The initiatives represent China's efforts to provide coordinated responses to challenges that transcend national borders, Mario Boselli, president of the Italy-China Foundation, said in a recent interview with Xinhua. They also represent a deepening of China's international vision following more than a decade of the Belt and Road Initiative, extending the focus from economic and infrastructure cooperation to development, security, dialogue among civilizations and global governance, he said. He believes that the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI) could offer opportunities to deepen cooperation between China and Europe, including Italy. The GDI's focus on climate change, the UN Sustainable Development Goals, digitalization and technological innovation could create opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy, photovoltaics and energy storage, among others, said Boselli. Italy and China can also strengthen cooperation among universities and research institutions in biotechnology, healthcare, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, he added. Noting that the GCI could promote cooperation in culture, heritage conservation, universities and youth exchanges, he said Italy, with its rich cultural heritage and the strong appeal of "Made in Italy" in China, is "one of the most natural European partners" for such initiatives. Taken together, the four initiatives outline a vision of a multipolar world with greater participation by emerging economies and countries of the Global South, Boselli said. With its tradition of dialogue with China and complementary economic strengths, Italy can play a bridging role between China and Europe, promoting practical cooperation in sustainable development, innovation, culture and global governance, he said. China's initiatives may not provide an immediate solution to current international tensions, but can offer "a space for reflection and dialogue" to identify more inclusive, practical and long-term forms of cooperation, he added. item.title: Chinese teenagers flock to tech frontline to touch the future amid AI study-tour boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Chinese teenagers flock to tech frontline to touch the future amid AI study-tour boom Children participate in a robot football competition in Jiyuan City, central China's Henan Province, Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Duan Erping/Xinhua) *To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. *Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. *AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a summer day, cheers erupted as clusters of children watched robots race across a soccer pitch, battling it out in playful matches, at a science center in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province. At a nearby workbench, nine-year-old Zhang Qihang was busy assembling a robot of his own. "Building robots is awesome! I can let my imagination run wild," he said, beaming with excitement. This was the scene at an artificial intelligence (AI) summer camp -- part of a new wave of study tours gaining traction across China. Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. A volunteer (2nd L) instructs a child how to assemble a robot in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, July 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ziheng) AI STUDY-TOUR BOOM During this summer vacation, AI-themed study tours have begun to gain ground, with bookings surging 370 percent year on year, according to online travel platform Ctrip. To tap into the growing demand for AI-focused tech tourism, a travel agency based in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, began adding visits to technology companies to its trip programs last summer. "On our Shanghai-Hangzhou independent study tours, AI-related activities now account for more than 80 percent of the itinerary," founder Zhu Ping said. The boom is unfolding against the backdrop of China's broader AI boom, powered by a wave of homegrown models and applications. For a growing number of Chinese teenagers, AI tools such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Doubao are becoming familiar companions in their everyday lives. The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, and the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177 billion U.S. dollars) during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of nearly 30 percent. Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report. To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. The goal is to help students understand and use AI properly, while sparking curiosity, nurturing creativity and honing their critical-thinking and problem-solving skills. Today, the AI study-tour wave is sweeping through China's schools, as primary and secondary schools incorporate it into their educational programs. Parents are taking their children into the heart of the tech industry to see how AI transforms the real world. China's tech-tourism boom is also drawing international visitors keen to get a close-up look at the innovation behind "Made in China." Since opening in Shanghai in May, Unitree Robotics's first embodied intelligence experience store in Asia has attracted many foreign visitors. Victoria, from Denmark, visited the store last month. "I've seen some of the dancing videos, but it's really cool to see them in real life," she said, viewing the development of AI and robotics in China as "revolutionary, new and exciting." A Russian tourist interacts with a robot at a store of Unitree Robotics in Beijing, capital of China, April 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong) FROM AI USERS TO AI CREATORS Today's children are growing up as AI natives, already fluent in AI tools. But AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. For Liang Yiduo, a Beijing middle school student, an AI summer camp run by internet giant NetEase offered a fresh perspective on the AI technology he thought he already knew. "I realized that large language models aren't just chatbots or simple tools," he said. "They can be assistants that work alongside you and help you create things tailored to your needs, like 'claws.'" "The goal of the study camp is to help children move from simply using AI to understanding it, creating with it and even building their own AI agents," said Wang Lijin, director and founder of Beijing Venus Future Education Consulting Center, which assists NetEase in running its study camps. Students attending a summer camp control a robot at an AI robot technology experience center in Shanghai, east China, July 19, 2026. (Photo by Zhang Xu/Xinhua) Some study tour organizers design programs around students' interests and abilities, aiming to spark curiosity and encourage deeper thinking. Shanghai Qingbao Robot Co., Ltd., for example, offers students who enjoy building things the chance to assemble robotic arms and explore the mechanics of shoulder and neck structures. It also gives students a comparative look at the robotics and AI industries in China, the US, Europe and Japan, helping them gain a more balanced understanding of China's strengths and shortcomings. Wang Lei, the company's chairman, believes that study tours can greatly broaden students' horizons in science and innovation. "Through immersive study tours, students start thinking for themselves about how robotics can be applied to everyday life, from unmanned retail to automated pharmacies," he said. Some students are taking it a step further, learning to spot real-world problems and use AI to develop solutions. In the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, a group of students spent six days in a camp turning ideas into an AI-powered product. "I've realized that learning AI isn't about showing off what I can do with it, but about using it to solve real problems for others," said one team member. "I want to keep learning AI so I can help more people in the future." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Regular Guangzhou-Shenzhen maritime cultural tourism route officially launched in south China
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
Regular Guangzhou-Shenzhen maritime cultural tourism route officially launched in south China The cruise ship Da Wan Qu Yi Dun docks at the Nansha International Cruise Home Port in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Aug. 22, 2026. Named after the Greater Bay Area, known in Chinese as Da Wan Qu, the cruise ship Da Wan Qu Yi Dun departed from the Nansha International Cruise Home Port in Guangzhou on Saturday, marking the official launch of the regular Guangzhou-Shenzhen maritime cultural tourism route. Sailing past the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, the Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link and 16 landmarks of the Greater Bay Area, the ship also provided visitors with diverse onboard experiences including performances themed on intangible cultural heritage and magic shows.
